title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: Vronsky and Anna spent the whole summer and part of the winter in the country, living in exactly the same situation and still taking no steps to obtain a divorce. They had an unspoken agreement not to go anywhere; but the longer they lived on their own — especially in the autumn, with no guests in the house — the more clearly both of them felt that they could not keep this up, and that something would have to change.

Their life looked as if nothing better could be wished for. They had abundance of everything; they had a child; and both had something to occupy them. Anna paid just as much attention to her appearance when there were no visitors, and she read a great deal — both novels and whatever serious literature was in fashion. She ordered every book praised in the foreign newspapers and reviews she received, and read them with that concentrated attention you only give to what you read in seclusion. On top of that, she studied in books and specialist journals every subject Vronsky took an interest in, so that he often went straight to her with questions about agriculture or architecture, sometimes even about horse-breeding or sport. He was amazed at her knowledge, her memory — at first he was inclined to doubt it, to ask her to back up her facts; and she would find what he wanted in some book and show him.

The hospital project interested her too. She didn't just help — she planned and proposed a great deal herself. But her main thought was still about herself: how dear was she to Vronsky? how far could she make up to him for everything he had given up? Vronsky appreciated this drive not just to please but to serve him, which had become the sole aim of her life; but at the same time he was wearied by the loving snares she used to hold him fast. As time passed and he found himself caught in those snares more and more often, he had a steadily growing desire — not so much to escape them as to test whether they hindered his freedom. If it hadn't been for this growing desire to be free, not to have a scene every time he wanted to go into town for a meeting or a race, Vronsky would have been perfectly satisfied with his life. The role he had taken up — that of a wealthy landowner, one of a class that ought to be the heart of the Russian aristocracy — was entirely to his taste; and now, after six months in that character, he found it even more satisfying. And his management of his estate, which absorbed and occupied him more and more, was a real success. In spite of the enormous sums spent on the hospital, on machinery, on cows ordered from Switzerland and many other things, he was convinced he wasn't squandering his fortune but increasing it. On anything to do with income — the sales of timber, wheat, and wool, the letting of land — Vronsky was hard as rock, and knew how to hold his prices. In all large-scale operations on this estate and his others, he stuck to the simplest methods that involved no risk, and on the small details he was careful and exacting to an extreme. In spite of all the cunning and ingenuity of the German steward — who would try to tempt him into purchases by making his original estimate always far larger than was really needed, and then suggesting to Vronsky that the thing might be had cheaper, turning a profit — Vronsky didn't budge. He listened to his steward, cross-examined him, and only agreed to his suggestions when the implement to be ordered or built was the very newest sort, not yet known in Russia and likely to cause a stir. Apart from such exceptions, he was willing to spend more only where there was a surplus, and when he did spend he went into the smallest details and insisted on getting the very best for the money — so that the way he handled his affairs made it clear that he wasn't wasting his fortune but building it up.
In October there were provincial elections in the Kashinsky province, where the estates of Vronsky, Sviazhsky, Koznishev, Oblonsky, and a small piece of Levin's land lay.

These elections were drawing public attention because of several things to do with them, and because of the people taking part. They had been much talked about, and great preparations were under way. People who never attended elections were coming from Moscow, from Petersburg, and from abroad to be there. Vronsky had promised Sviazhsky some time before that he'd go. In the run-up to the elections Sviazhsky, who often dropped in at Vozdvizhenskoe, drove over to fetch him. The day before, there had been very nearly a quarrel between Vronsky and Anna over this proposed trip. It was the bleakest sort of autumn weather, which is so dreary in the country, and so, bracing himself for a fight, Vronsky, with a hard, cold expression, told Anna he was leaving in a tone he had never used with her before. To his surprise, Anna took the news with complete composure and only asked when he'd be back. He looked at her closely, unable to account for this calm. She smiled at his look. He knew that way she had of withdrawing into herself, and he knew it only happened when she had decided on something without letting him in on her plans. He was afraid of it; but he was so anxious to avoid a scene that he kept up appearances, and half sincerely believed in what he longed to believe — her reasonableness.
"I hope you won't be too bored?"
"I hope not," Anna said. "I got a box of books from Gautier's yesterday. No, I won't be bored."
"She's trying to take that tone, and so much the better," he thought, "or else it would be the same thing all over again."

And he set off for the elections without pressing her for a frank explanation. It was the first time since the start of their intimacy that he had parted from her without one. From one angle that troubled him; from another he felt it was better this way. "At first there will be, as this time, something undefined held back, and then she'll get used to it. I can give up anything for her — but not my masculine independence," he thought.
